result.summary: Difference-based preimage techniques are excluded at 20-21 rounds by an exact, verified structural count, not by extrapolation. The best conceivable chunk-separated MITM on 21-round SHA-256 with fixed IV costs 2^160 - eighty-three bits WORSE than our 2^77 - because SHA-256's message schedule makes W16..W20 depend on 13 of the 16 message words, capping the forward chunk's neutral freedom at exactly 3 words (96 bits). The published MITM/biclique corpus confirms the regime: every SHA-256 preimage attack ever published, at every step count from 24 to 52, lands between 2^240 and 2^255.6, i.e. a gain of 0.4 to 16 bits over brute force, and NOBODY has published a MITM or biclique preimage attack on SHA-256 below 24 steps. Rebound is a collision tool and cannot be converted: it controls differences, and a preimage is a value condition. The GF(2)-linearity observation in WHAT_WOULD_BE_NEEDED.md is true but buys nothing, because our attack is not blocked by inverting Sigma0 (the 16 GB table does that in one lookup) - it is blocked by two pure 2^-32 value filters, and the local differential lever against those was already measured and killed by the elimination search.
result.mechanism:
THE EXACT CALCULATION (part b, the decisive one). Our setting is a fixed-IV single-block compression-function preimage: the IV is fixed, so from the target digest the final state is fully known (digest = IV + state_R). Both endpoints of the 21-round map are therefore known, and splice-and-cut degenerates - there is no feed-forward freedom left to exploit. Any MITM must cut the 21 rounds at some round c, compute the 256-bit state S_c forward from IV using W_0..W_{c-1} and backward from the known end state using W_c..W_20, and match. Matching is on the full 256-bit state, so dm=256 is never the binding constraint; the cost is the standard 2^(n - min(df,db)) with n=256 (Guo et al., Sec. 4: total time 2^(n-2d)(2^d t1 + 2^d t2) = 2^(n-d)).

Independence requires the forward-neutral message words to be absent from the backward chunk. The backward chunk always contains rounds 16..20, hence the expanded words W16..W20, and these depend transitively on 13 of the 16 base words. Verified exactly and numerically (3000 random trials plus 200 single-bit flips per word): at R=21 the ONLY base words absent from W16..W20 are W6, W7, W8. So df <= 96 bits, full stop. Scanning all 20 cuts, the optimum is cut c=9: forward chunk = rounds 0..8 with neutral {W6,W7,W8} = 96 bits; backward chunk = rounds 9..20 with neutral {W9..W15} = 224 bits; W0..W5 are shared and must be public. Cost = 2^(256-96) = 2^160, memory 2^96.

This produces an exact ladder, 32 bits per round, that also explains the literature:
  R=19: untouched {4,5,6,7,8,12,13}, best min(df,db)=160 -> MITM 2^96   (ours 2^15.25)
  R=20: untouched {5,6,7,8,13},      best min(df,db)=128 -> MITM 2^128  (ours 2^45.4)
  R=21: untouched {6,7,8},           best min(df,db)=96  -> MITM 2^160  (ours 2^77)
  R=22: untouched {7,8}                                  -> MITM 2^192
  R=23: untouched {8}                                    -> MITM 2^224
  R=24: untouched {} (all 16 words feed W16..W23)        -> MITM 2^256
The gap to our attack is essentially constant: 80.8, 82.6, 83.0 bits at R=19,20,21. The R=24 entry independently validates the model: chunk separation dies exactly at 24 steps, which is precisely why Isobe-Shibutani's 24-step attack had to buy its 16 bits with splice-and-cut plus partial matching rather than plain separation, and why no MITM below 24 steps has ever been published - there is nothing for MITM to gain there that a direct algebraic solve does not already take.

To beat 2^77 a MITM would need min(df,db,dm) >= 179 bits, i.e. >= 5.6 mutually disjoint neutral message words on EACH side out of 16, when 13 of the 16 are coupled through W16..W20. The maximum available is 3 words on the light side. This is a hard cap on the technique, not a limit of our search.

WHY THE PUBLISHED TECHNIQUES CANNOT LIFT IT. (i) Initial structures / bicliques / partial-fixing add DOF at the bit level, but the published magnitudes are single digits: Guo et al.'s DOF column for SHA-256 is 3-10 bits at 43-47 steps, KRS's SHA-256 biclique has dimension 1, and their 11-round biclique text states "degree of freedom is only 1 bit". Isobe-Shibutani's 16 bits at 24 steps is the record DOF for SHA-256 at ANY step count. Even granting a wildly generous full extra word (+32 bits) at R=21 gives 2^128, still 51 bits worse than 2^77. (ii) Bit-level partial neutrality is a zero-sum trade here: a word entering W16..W20 only through a modular addition has a few high bits neutral for the low bits of the expanded word, but the backward chunk needs all of it, so you must shrink dm by the same amount - this is exactly the partial-fixing/partial-matching trade-off and it does not move min(df,db,dm). (iii) The splice-and-cut / pseudo-preimage line is a DIFFERENT problem (free chaining value) and does not solve ours at all; converting it to a real hash preimage costs 2^((n+t)/2 + 1) >= 2^129 for n=256 even with a free pseudo-preimage (t=0), so that whole line is floored 52 bits above 2^77 regardless of step count. (iv) Wagner k-tree / generalized birthday does not apply: it needs the matching condition to decompose as a sum of independent functions of disjoint variable blocks, and the SHA-256 round chain does not decompose that way.

(c) REBOUND. Rebound (Mendel-Rechberger-Schlaeffer-Thomsen, FSE 2009) is structurally a collision tool for three reasons, each of which would have to be repaired separately. First, its object is a PAIR conforming to a truncated differential characteristic; the inbound phase spends middle freedom to satisfy the expensive segment with amortised cost 1, and the outbound is probabilistic in the DIFFERENCE. A preimage is a condition on an absolute 256-bit VALUE, and a differential characteristic imposes no condition whatsoever on the output value: the conforming set is ~2^(512-w) messages (w = sufficient conditions) whose 256-bit outputs are uniform, so hitting the target still costs 2^256 per conforming message, i.e. rebound gives 0 bits toward a preimage by construction. Our own project measured this uniformity independently (no linear or affine structure in the residuals beyond three carry-free LSB relations). Second, the inbound phase is powered by inverting a differential over an S-box layer via a differential distribution table; SHA-256 is ARX with no S-box, so the SHA-2 analogue is Mendel-Nad-Schlaeffer-style local-collision search, which tops out at 31-step practical collisions / 39-step semi-free-start (Alamgir-Nejati-Bright 2024 reproduce 38 with SAT+CAS), all collisions, none preimages. Third, the ONE place where differentials genuinely become a preimage tool is the biclique - KRS build the biclique's 2^(2d) states from a Delta-trail and a nabla-trail - and that is already covered above: it is an MITM amplifier worth d bits with d=1..3, so it would take 2^160 to about 2^157.

(a) THE COMPLEMENTARY-DIFFICULTY ARGUMENT IS BASED ON A MISDIAGNOSIS. WHAT_WOULD_BE_NEEDED.md reasons that Sigma0/sigma0 block us on values but are free for XOR differences. Both halves are true and the conclusion still fails, because inverting sigma0 is NOT our bottleneck: the 16 GB table inverts u -> sigma0(u)-u in one lookup and the three lookups cost 2^0 each. What costs bits at R=21 is (i) the 2^13.4 collapse loss and (ii) two independent pure 2^-32 filters c3=0 and c4=0 on quantities already fully determined by a0 and the context. The only way a difference technique attacks those is a neutral-word/message-modification lever: find a perturbation that moves c3 (and c4) without moving C0,C1,C2. That is precisely a single-bit XOR-difference propagation measurement, and the elimination search already ran it at full width: every free word moves all of KC0,KC1,KC2 and kappa3 by 10.6-16.1 bits per flipped bit, against the 2 bits absorption needs, over ~1.6M legal context conditions and 105M reduced-width assignments. So the differential lever in its only usable local form has been tested here, contrary to the specification's claim that the family is untouched - it was tested under a different name.

With a wildly generous extra full word of bit-level partial-fixing freedom (df=128, unattainable), 2^128, still 51 bits worse. result.mechanism:
Three findings, in order of force.

FIRST, the two domains are the same frame. The map W_0..W_15 -> a_0..a_15 is a bijection and it is prefix-triangular: a_r depends only on W_0..W_r. Fixing a prefix of W is therefore identical to fixing a prefix of a, so every W-coordinate frame with a prefix context is a translate of the published a-frame, and those were already priced at 45.3-45.4 bits. The counting is literally identical, not merely equal: at R=20 the digest's 8 words split as 4 determinations (they fix W_12..W_15 given the context) plus 4 constraints (W_16..W_19, which the schedule also determines). That is 12 free words against 4 constraints in both descriptions. The a-frame is not a different count from the W-frame; it is the W-frame with the digest optimally spent. Worth recording separately: the published solver already performs its three lookups in message coordinates — the table returns W_1, W_2, W_3 and a_1, a_2, a_3 are back-solved (submask_family.py lines 379-398). The a-words are bookkeeping around a W-domain inversion.

SECOND, the absorption structure the a-domain has is a property of a-coordinates and does not exist in W-coordinates. The absorber works because a_k enters exactly two recovered message words linearly, W_k with +1 and W_{k+8} with -1, and the schedule pairs W_{t-15} (under sigma0) with W_{t-7} (linear) at exactly that distance of 8, so C_j reads sigma0(X) - X with X = W_{j+1}. In the message domain the analogous linear pair is W_i into W_{i+7} and W_{i+16}, both with coefficient +1 — same sign, so no sigma0(u)-u atom forms. Measured: zero exact +/-1 linear entries among the 128 (W_i, digest residual) cells at R=20 and R=21, and an exhaustive translate-class test at four reduced widths finds zero absorbable cells there too, while the same test reproduces the a-domain diagonal a_1->C0, a_2->C1, a_3->C2, a_4->C3 exactly and correctly rejects a_5. The W-domain's absorbers are precisely W_i with i >= R-4, the last four message words — which is to say, precisely what the backward chain already peels for free. Their count is max(0, 20-R) as a matching: 3 at R=17, 2 at R=18, 1 at R=19, 0 at R=20. The requirement is 8. The message domain runs out of absorbers before 20 rounds, and would need R <= 12 to have enough.

THIRD, the hybrid is strictly worse, not merely equal. Keeping the backward chain but parameterising the 12 free words as W_0..W_11 gives zero absorbable cells at R=19, 20 and 21 — it destroys even the working C_0 <- a_1 absorber. The cause is not subtle and I confirmed it with a pinned-context control: a_4..a_11 and a_0..a_3 are independent coordinates, but fixing W_2..W_11 does not fix a_2..a_11. Varying W_1 drags a_2, a_3 and hence the whole context along, and the context reaches C_0 through W_14 and W_16. The state words are the coordinates in which the context can be frozen; the message words are not.

The reason this is not an accident of SHA-256's schedule: the W-domain frame's counting is round-independent — 16 unknowns against 8 digest constraints at every R >= 16. If absorption worked there it would break the full function, not a reduced one. The a-frame's count degrades with R (12 free / 4 constraints at 20, 13 / 5 at 21), which is exactly why it is a reduced-round attack. Round-independence is the signature that the entire difficulty sits in the avalanche rather than the counting, and the avalanche is full: minimum edge weight over all 128 cells is 7.69 bits at R=20 and 14.52 at R=21, against a 2-bit absorption threshold.

Finally, this domain is not in fact unexamined — only unexamined by this project. Parameterising by message words with a few chosen as neutral IS the meet-in-the-middle preimage framework of Aoki, Guo, Matusiewicz, Sasaki and Wang (their neutral words are W_16 and W_19), the most heavily worked family for step-reduced SHA-2. It reaches 42 steps at 2^251.7 — 206 bits worse at 20 rounds than what the state-word frame already achieves.
result.next_test:
Do not spend more compute on single-word absorption in the message domain; it is closed at four widths and at full width. The one generalisation that is genuinely unrun, and that the near-miss at a_5 argues for, is PAIRWISE absorption: the a_5 obstruction is that C_1 depends on a_2 and a_5 only through the combination Y = a_2 - Sigma0(a_5) (e_6 = a_2 + a_6 - Sigma0(a_5) - Maj(a_5,a_4,a_3), with Maj constant in the family), so a single lookup recovers Y but not either word. Every test in this project, mine included, asks whether one constraint absorbs one unknown. The untested question is whether some constraint R_j and some pair (u,v) admit R_j = F(u + g(v)) + s with F universal — a two-word absorber that a one-axis table still inverts. At w=6 this is exhaustively decidable (64 values per word, 120 word pairs, 8 or 4 constraints) in well under thirty minutes with redw.py's translate_equiv generalised to search g over the natural candidate set {identity, Sigma0, Sigma1, sigma0, sigma1, negation}; the positive control is Y = a_2 - Sigma0(a_5) against C_1, which must come back ABS. If the enumeration returns only combinations that are already known, the pairwise level is closed too and the table-absorption paradigm can be declared exhausted at the level of pairs as well as singletons. Prediction, from what I measured: it returns only the a_5/C_1 combination and its translates, because breaking a two-word absorber into its constituents still requires a third relation, and that is the cycle the barrier paper already prices.

Two things I deliberately did not spend the budget on, and why. Angle A (differences through the GF(2)-linear maps) is the complementary profile and belongs to another explorer. The offset-alignment idea that fell out of this analysis — W_i reaches the next rounds through Sigma0(a_i) and Sigma1(a_i + c) with DIFFERENT offsets, which is what forces a two-axis table, and the tie a_8 = T2(a_7,a_6,a_5) makes e_8 = a_4 and aligns them into a single-axis one-input function — I did price, because it lies outside the condition menu the elimination search enumerated. It does not cut: the a_4 -> C_0 edge falls only from 12.44 to 11.65 bits, against the 2-bit threshold. Making the dependence single-axis is not the same as making it mild, and C_0 is already spent absorbing a_1. Closed.

EXACT COST LAWS (measured, part a). Linear layer: Sigma0, Sigma1, sigma0, sigma1 all satisfy f(x^d)=f(x)^f(d) with 0 violations in 1,048,576 trials each — free, exact. Modular addition: P[(a^d)+b == (a+b)^d] = 2^-hw(d & 0x7fffffff), measured against 15 values of d and matching to <=0.06 bits; the MSB is exactly free (d=0x80000000 gives p=1.000000, d=0xffffffff gives 0 of 2^20). This is Lipmaa-Moriai xdp+ specialised to beta=0, gamma=alpha. Ch: exact 8x8 enumeration gives cost 0 bits at input-difference patterns 000 and 011 (in 011 the f and g differences cancel through the selector), 1 bit at the other six. Maj: cost 0 at 000 and 111, 1 bit at the other six. Per-round accounting at 21 rounds: 52 free linear maps (2 per round + 2 per expansion step) against 162 charged modular additions (7 per round: h+Sigma1(e), +Ch, +K free, +W, Sigma0(a)+Maj, T1+T2, d+T1; plus 3 per expansion step). That is the complementary profile in one line — and the charged side outnumbers the free side 3:1.

WHY IT DOES NOT CONVERT (part b). With a fixed IV the chaining input difference is 0, so any difference that maps a preimage to a preimage of the SAME digest must give zero output difference: it is exactly a fixed-IV collision. Three ways to turn a characteristic into preimage advantage, all closed here. (i) Biclique: the literature ceiling for this entire family on SHA-256 is 45 steps at 2^255.5 (Khovratovich-Rechberger-Savelieva, FSE 2012 / eprint 2011/286) — 0.5 bits under brute force. To matter against our 2^77 the biclique dimension would have to be ~30; bicliques on SHA-2 deliver <1. (ii) Differential MITM: needs the computation to split into two independently computable halves. Our per-candidate cost is three data-dependent random accesses into a 16 GB table; there is no arithmetic for a MITM to split. (iii) A solution-to-solution map: a d with F(W^d)=F(W) for a non-negligible fraction of W. That is what I tested directly, and it is 0.

FREEDOM ACCOUNTING (why (iii) cannot work even in principle). If the best 21-step trail for a given d costs c bits, the fraction of messages following it is 2^-c, so among the ~2^256 preimages of a fixed target the expected number that also follow it is 2^(256-c). Existence is plausible; reaching one requires imposing the c trail conditions ON TOP of the 256 digest conditions, a strictly more constrained search than the preimage search we already run. And amplification — many preimages from one — does not lower the cost of the FIRST, which is the bar. This is why the two facts sit together without contradiction: 21-step collisions are cheap, and 21-step preimages are not moved by them at all.

FILTER CHECK against R1-R5 of the specification. The difference frame does pass R1 (it never inverts Sigma0 of an unknown jointly with modular addition — that was the whole point of the observation). It fails on a requirement the specification did not state, because the specification was scoped to value-based table absorption: a characteristic does not fix a digest. That gap should be added to the spec as R6.

ONE ARTEFACT, DIAGNOSED AND DISMISSED. At 19 rounds single-bit differences in W15 give mean |dDigest| = 88-90 of 256 instead of 128, and the weight-2 family reaches 60 — an 8.5-sigma-looking outlier. It is not differential structure: W15 is active only in rounds 15 and 17 of 19, so the avalanche is simply incomplete. At 21 rounds every one of the 16 per-word means is 126-130 and every per-word minimum is 105-119, matching full avalanche. BOTH GAPS CLOSED. gain_bits = 0. Cost at 21 rounds unchanged at 2^77 (2^45.4 at 20, 2^15.25 at 19).

The two "untested" directions named in WHAT_WOULD_BE_NEEDED.md are no longer untested, and neither is a gap in the barrier — one is priced 83 bits on the wrong side of it, the other turns out not to be a second frame at all.

(A) Difference-based techniques. The complementary-difficulty observation in the spec is exactly true and buys exactly nothing, for a reason the spec did not anticipate: this attack is not blocked by inverting Sigma0/sigma0 (the 16 GB table does that in one lookup at cost 2^0); it is blocked by two pure 2^-32 value filters. Differences cannot see a value filter. Three independent measurements agree: (i) the best chunk-separated MITM at 21 rounds costs 2^160, 83 bits worse than 2^77, from an exact and now twice-verified structural cap; (ii) the best zero-in/zero-out characteristic reachable in the frame where Sigma0/sigma0 are free costs 2^-2889 at 21 rounds against a 2^-77 bar, because the charged modular additions outnumber the free linear maps 3:1 (162 vs 52 per 21 rounds); (iii) applied directly to the five witnesses we own, 13,981,848 nonzero XOR differences gave 0 second preimages, 95% bound p <= 2^-22.2. W_0..W_15 -> a_0..a_15 is a prefix-triangular bijection (verified 300/300 both directions), so a W-prefix context IS an a-prefix context and the counting is identical, not merely comparable (12 free words / 4 constraints at R=20 in both). Measured: 0 of 128 exact +/-1 cells at R=20 and R=21, minimum edge weight 7.69 / 14.52 bits, 0 absorbable cells at four reduced widths with the a-domain diagonal correctly reproduced as positive control. The W-domain's only absorbers are the last four message words — what the backward chain already peels free — and they run out at R=20 (count max(0, 20-R), requirement 8). The hybrid is worse still: 0 absorbable cells at R=19, 20, 21, because varying W_1 drags a_2, a_3 and the whole context with it.

result.plain_english: Our attack works by guessing one 32-bit word and then reading three more straight out of a big lookup table, which leaves two 32-bit conditions to be hit by luck. The last note we wrote said there were two places we had not looked: techniques based on differences between two messages rather than on the values themselves, and describing the attack in terms of the message words instead of the internal state words. Three separate investigations have now looked at both, and both are closed. Difference-based methods do sail straight through the operation that blocks us — that part of the note was right — but it turns out that operation was never our bottleneck; our lookup table already handles it in a single step. What actually costs us is having to hit two exact 32-bit values, and a difference-based method says nothing about values at all: it relates one message to another, while a preimage attack has to land on one specific fixed digest and has no second message to relate to. When priced out properly, the best method of that kind costs about 2^160 at 21 rounds against our 2^77 — eighty-three bits on the wrong side, and the gap stays the same size at 19, 20 and 21 rounds because it comes from a hard structural cap in SHA-256's message schedule rather than from anything we failed to try. Applying nearly fourteen million differences to the preimages we already own produced not a single new one. The message-word idea failed for a cleaner reason: it is not a second point of view at all. The map from message words to state words is a triangular one-to-one correspondence, so fixing message words is fixing state words, and the two descriptions give literally the same count of unknowns and constraints. Where they differ, the message description is worse — the trick our attack depends on exists only because of a particular plus-one/minus-one sign pattern in the state coordinates, and in message coordinates both signs are plus, so the trick cannot form. Every measurement of it comes back at 8 to 15 bits where 2 would be needed. The honest conclusion is that the barrier we described is wider than we claimed: it is not only a barrier to value-based table tricks, it also holds against the difference-based family and against re-describing the problem in message coordinates. Nothing here changes the published attack or its numbers; it changes what we can honestly say about how far the wall extends, and it means the note's closing paragraph — which invites a reader to go try these two things — now has to be rewritten to say that we tried them and what they cost.

## The two remaining gaps, now closed

The previous version of this note named two untested directions.  Three further
searches have now tested both.  Neither yields a bit, and the second turns out
not to be a separate direction at all.

**Differences.**  `Sigma0` and `sigma0` are GF(2)-linear, so an exclusive-or
difference passes through them exactly and for free
(`Sigma0(x XOR d) = Sigma0(x) XOR Sigma0(d)`, 0 violations in 1,048,576 trials
per function), while the modular additions this attack handles for free are what
carries make hard for differences.  That observation is exactly true and buys
exactly nothing, because it misdiagnoses the bottleneck: inverting `sigma0` is
**not** what costs us -- the 16 GB table inverts `u -> sigma0(u) - u` in one
lookup at cost 2^0.  What costs bits is the 2^13.4 collapse loss and two
independent pure 2^-32 *value* filters, and a difference says nothing about a
value (R6).  Measured three ways.  *Arithmetically*: modular addition costs
exactly `hw(d & 0x7fffffff)` bits (matched to <=0.06 bits over fifteen values of
`d`, MSB exactly free), `Ch` and `Maj` cost 0 bits at two of eight input patterns
and 1 bit at the other six, and 21 rounds charge 162 modular additions against
only 52 free linear maps -- the charged side outnumbers the free side three to
one.  The zero-output message-difference space has dimension exactly 256 at
`R = 19, 20, 21`, but every element has Hamming weight around 256 of 512 and is
annihilated by the first modular addition (0 of 4096 messages followed any of 120
sampled kernel trails past round 0); even a single active bit costs 2 bits at
injection, ~14 bits cumulative one round later, and had 0 survivors of 4,194,304
messages two rounds on.  The best characteristic found costs `2^-2376`,
`2^-2631`, `2^-2889` at `R = 19, 20, 21` against a `2^-77` bar.
*Structurally*: at 21 steps differentials are far **easier** than this attack --
practical fixed-IV collisions reach 28 steps, 31 at `2^65.5`, 37 in 2025 -- and
they still buy nothing, precisely because of R6.  *Directly*: 13,981,848 nonzero
differences (weight 1 and 2 exhaustively, all 65,535 MSB-only subsets, two
million random weight 3--8, and both GF(2) kernels at their verified dimensions)
applied to five verified witnesses -- both 20-round preimages including the
all-ones target and three 19-round ones -- gave **0** second preimages, 95% bound
`p <= 2^-22.2`.  The published conversions are closed as well: bicliques are a
meet-in-the-middle amplifier worth their dimension, and the published dimension
for SHA-256 is 1--3 ("degree of freedom is only 1 bit"), so fact 6's `2^160`
becomes about `2^157`; pseudo-preimage conversion is floored at
`2^{(256+t)/2+1} >= 2^129` even for a free pseudo-preimage; and rebound is a

one local form that could touch *this* attack -- a perturbation moving `c3`

## How to use this

For a referee or a reader, this is the honest statement of scope, and it is now
wider than it was: the barrier is sharp, single-edged and measured, and it is a
barrier to value-based table absorption, to the difference-based family, and to
re-parameterisation in message coordinates -- but still to a named set of
techniques rather than to the problem.  For anyone continuing the work, R1--R7
are the filter to apply to a new idea *before* spending compute on it.  What
remains genuinely unrun is narrow and predicted to fail: **pairwise** absorption
(does some constraint `R_j` and some pair `(u,v)` admit `R_j = F(u + g(v)) + s`
with `F` universal?  positive control `Y = a2 - Sigma0(a5)` against `C1`, which
must return ABS), and a meet-in-the-middle split applied to the five-constraint
system `C0..C4` on 13 free words rather than to the round chain.  Both are under
thirty minutes of CPU.  Do not spend further compute on characteristic search,
on meet-in-the-middle, biclique or rebound against the round chain, or on
single-word absorption in the message domain.
